claim: Multiple neural circuits involved in behavioral inhibition converge upon the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
source: Multiple neural circuits involved in behavioral inhibition converge upon a key basal ganglia output nucleus, the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established context for the study.

claim: Action restraint is visible as direction-selective slowing of reaction times.
source: This action restraint – visible as direction-selective slowing of reaction times – altered both rates and patterns of SNr spiking.
evidence: The manuscript defines action restraint operationally through behavioral measurement.

claim: Overall SNr firing rate was elevated before the Go! cue during proactive inhibition.
source: Overall firing rate was elevated before the Go! cue, and this effect was driven by a subpopulation of direction-selective SNr neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The elevation in SNr firing rate before the Go! cue was driven by a subpopulation of direction-selective SNr neurons.
source: Overall firing rate was elevated before the Go! cue, and this effect was driven by a subpopulation of direction-selective SNr neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2F-G.

claim: In neural state space, proactive inhibition corresponded to a shift away from the restrained movement.
source: In neural state space, this corresponded to a shift away from the restrained movement.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through state-space analysis in Figure 3.

claim: SNr neurons showed more variable inter-spike intervals during proactive inhibition.
source: SNr neurons also showed more variable inter-spike intervals during proactive inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: More variable inter-spike intervals corresponded to more variable state-space trajectories.
source: This corresponded to more variable state-space trajectories, which may slow reaction times via reduced preparation to move.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: More variable state-space trajectories may slow reaction times via reduced preparation to move.
source: This corresponded to more variable state-space trajectories, which may slow reaction times via reduced preparation to move.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation stated in the abstract.

claim: Behavioral inhibition is central to cognitive control.
source: This capacity for behavioral inhibition is considered central to cognitive control (Bari and Robbins, 2013), and is compromised in a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders (Chambers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Behavioral inhibition is compromised in a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders.
source: This capacity for behavioral inhibition is considered central to cognitive control (Bari and Robbins, 2013), and is compromised in a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders (Chambers et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Reactive inhibition involves fast cue responses in frontal cortex and basal ganglia pathways.
source: Reactive inhibition has been shown to involve fast cue responses in frontal cortex and basal ganglia pathways (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Wager et al., 2005), including from the subthalamic nucleus (STN) to SNr (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Reactive inhibition involves fast cue responses from the subthalamic nucleus (STN) to SNr.
source: Reactive inhibition has been shown to involve fast cue responses in frontal cortex and basal ganglia pathways (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Wager et al., 2005), including from the subthalamic nucleus (STN) to SNr (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Rapid response to stimuli can transiently and broadly retard action initiation.
source: This rapid response to stimuli can transiently, and broadly, retard action initiation, providing time for a second set of basal ganglia mechanisms to cancel actions (Mallet et al., 2016; Schmidt and Berke, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Proactive inhibition refers to an altered state of preparation in which particular actions are restrained.
source: By contrast, 'proactive' inhibition refers to an altered state of preparation, in which particular actions are restrained (Cai et al., 2011; Claffey et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Proactive inhibition is behaviorally apparent as longer reaction times selectively for the restrained action.
source: Proactive inhibition has been argued to be especially important for human life (Aron, 2011), and is behaviorally apparent as longer reaction times (RTs) selectively for the restrained action.
evidence: This is stated as an established behavioral signature.

claim: Proactive inhibition has been argued to be especially important for human life.
source: Proactive inhibition has been argued to be especially important for human life (Aron, 2011), and is behaviorally apparent as longer reaction times (RTs) selectively for the restrained action.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Proactive inhibition has been proposed to involve the pathway from striatum 'indirectly' to SNr, via globus pallidus pars externa (GPe).
source: The underlying mechanisms are not well understood, but have been proposed (Aron, 2011) to involve the pathway from striatum 'indirectly' to SNr, via globus pallidus pars externa (GPe).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: The state of being prepared to stop did not involve an overall net change in GPe firing rate.
source: In a prior study (Gu et al., 2020) we therefore recorded from GPe neurons as rats engaged proactive inhibition toward a specific action. The state of being prepared to stop did not involve an overall net change in GPe firing rate, but rather a shift at the level of neural population dynamics away from action initiation, and toward the alternative action.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the same authors.

claim: The state of being prepared to stop involved a shift at the level of GPe neural population dynamics away from action initiation, and toward the alternative action.
source: In a prior study (Gu et al., 2020) we therefore recorded from GPe neurons as rats engaged proactive inhibition toward a specific action. The state of being prepared to stop did not involve an overall net change in GPe firing rate, but rather a shift at the level of neural population dynamics away from action initiation, and toward the alternative action.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the same authors.

claim: Basal ganglia output neurons are thought to affect behavior not just via their firing rates, but also via their firing patterns and synchrony.
source: Basal ganglia output neurons are thought to affect behavior not just via their firing rates, but also via their firing patterns and synchrony (Rubin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is associated with an increase in firing variability and synchronous bursting, often without rate changes.
source: In particular, Parkinson's disease (PD) is associated with an increase in firing variability and synchronous bursting, often without rate changes (Lobb, 2014; Willard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Parkinson's disease is characterized by slowed movement initiation.
source: As PD is characterized by slowed movement initiation (Low et al., 2002), we assessed whether related physiological changes are present when movements are slowed as the result of proactive inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Rats responded to Go! cues with rapid leftward or rightward movements.
source: Rats responded to Go! cues with rapid leftward or rightward movements, but also prepared to cancel one of these movement directions on trials when a Stop! cue might occur.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task used in the study.

claim: Rats prepared to cancel one of the movement directions on trials when a Stop! cue might occur.
source: Rats responded to Go! cues with rapid leftward or rightward movements, but also prepared to cancel one of these movement directions on trials when a Stop! cue might occur.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task design.

claim: Rats needed to maintain their position in the start port for a variable delay (500–1250 ms, uniform distribution) until a Go! cue was presented.
source: To proceed, they need to maintain this position for a variable delay (500–1250 ms, uniform distribution) until a Go! cue is presented (1 or 4 kHz tone, indicating a leftward or rightward movement, respectively).
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: A 1 kHz tone indicated a leftward movement and a 4 kHz tone indicated a rightward movement.
source: To proceed, they need to maintain this position for a variable delay (500–1250 ms, uniform distribution) until a Go! cue is presented (1 or 4 kHz tone, indicating a leftward or rightward movement, respectively).
evidence: This describes the task cue structure.

claim: If the movement was initiated rapidly after the Go! cue (RT limit <800 ms) and completed correctly and promptly (movement time limit, MT <500 ms), rats were rewarded with a sugar pellet.
source: If the movement is initiated rapidly after the Go! cue (RT limit <800 ms), and completed correctly and promptly (movement time limit, MT <500 ms), rats are rewarded with a sugar pellet dispensed at a separate food hopper.
evidence: This describes the task reward contingencies.

claim: On a subset of trials, the Go! cue was followed by a Stop! cue (white noise burst; delay after Go! cue onset = 100–250 ms).
source: On a subset of trials, the Go! cue is followed by a Stop! cue (white noise burst; delay after Go! cue onset = 100–250 ms).
evidence: This describes the task structure for stop trials.

claim: The Stop! cue indicated that the rat should not initiate a movement, and instead hold their nose in the Center port for at least 800 ms to trigger reward delivery.
source: This indicates that the rat should not initiate a movement, and instead hold their nose in the Center port for at least 800 ms (after Go! cue onset) to trigger reward delivery.
evidence: This describes the task requirements for stop trials.

claim: The three possible start ports were associated with different Stop! cue probabilities.
source: To probe selective proactive inhibition, the three possible start ports were associated with different Stop! cue probabilities (counterbalanced across rats; Gu et al., 2020, Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This describes the task design for probing selective proactive inhibition.

claim: SNr microelectrode recordings were obtained from 10 rats that had successfully learned the proactive task.
source: We obtained SNr microelectrode recordings from rats (n=10) that had successfully learned this proactive task, as indicated by significant and selective slowing of RTs for movements contraversive to the implant side (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and inclusion criteria.

claim: Successful learning of the proactive task was indicated by significant and selective slowing of RTs for movements contraversive to the implant side.
source: We obtained SNr microelectrode recordings from rats (n=10) that had successfully learned this proactive task, as indicated by significant and selective slowing of RTs for movements contraversive to the implant side (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the behavioral criterion for task learning.

claim: 60 sessions showed significant proactive inhibition effect.
source: In the same rats we compared SNr activity in sessions in which this proactive effect was significant (n=60), to sessions in which it was not (n=25; Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the number of sessions with the behavioral effect.

claim: 25 sessions did not show significant proactive inhibition effect.
source: In the same rats we compared SNr activity in sessions in which this proactive effect was significant (n=60), to sessions in which it was not (n=25; Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the number of sessions without the behavioral effect.

claim: Sessions with significant proactive inhibition effect showed RT slowing selectively for the Maybe-Stop direction (Wilcoxon signed rank tests on median RTs of Maybe-Stop-Contra versus No-Stop: Contra cues: z=6.8, p=1.1 × 10-11).
source: The sessions with significant proactive inhibition effect show RT slowing selectively for the Maybe-Stop direction (Wilcoxon signed rank tests on median RTs of Maybe-Stop-Contra versus No-Stop: Contra cues: z=6.8, p=1.1 × 10-11), but not for the other direction (Ipsi cues: z=–1.2, p=0.22) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral data analysis.

claim: Sessions with significant proactive inhibition effect did not show RT slowing for the Ipsi direction (Ipsi cues: z=–1.2, p=0.22).
source: The sessions with significant proactive inhibition effect show RT slowing selectively for the Maybe-Stop direction (Wilcoxon signed rank tests on median RTs of Maybe-Stop-Contra versus No-Stop: Contra cues: z=6.8, p=1.1 × 10-11), but not for the other direction (Ipsi cues: z=–1.2, p=0.22) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral data analysis.

claim: On Maybe-Stop-Contra trials rats were more likely to fail to respond quickly enough (RT limit errors; Wilcoxon signed rank tests, z=6.4, p=1.5 × 10-10).
source: Additionally, on Maybe-Stop-Contra trials rats were more likely to fail to respond quickly enough (RT limit errors; Wilcoxon signed rank tests, z=6.4, p=1.5 × 10-10) and to select the wrong choice (i.e. not matching the Go! cue; Wilcoxon signed rank tests, z=6.5, p=1.1 × 10-10).
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral data analysis.

claim: On Maybe-Stop-Contra trials rats were more likely to select the wrong choice (Wilcoxon signed rank tests, z=6.5, p=1.1 × 10-10).
source: Additionally, on Maybe-Stop-Contra trials rats were more likely to fail to respond quickly enough (RT limit errors; Wilcoxon signed rank tests, z=6.4, p=1.5 × 10-10) and to select the wrong choice (i.e. not matching the Go! cue; Wilcoxon signed rank tests, z=6.5, p=1.1 × 10-10).
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral data analysis.

claim: 446 SNr neurons were recorded during sessions with significant proactive inhibition.
source: We examined the activity of individual SNr neurons (n=446; mean firing rate = 38 Hz, locations are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) recorded during the sessions with significant proactive inhibition.
evidence: This describes the sample size for neural recordings.

claim: The mean firing rate of recorded SNr neurons was 38 Hz.
source: We examined the activity of individual SNr neurons (n=446; mean firing rate = 38 Hz, locations are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) recorded during the sessions with significant proactive inhibition.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the neural data.

claim: Average firing rates were significantly higher in the Maybe-Stop-Contra condition before the Go! cue.
source: Average firing rates were significantly higher in the Maybe-Stop-Contra condition (Figure 2A, top), and this difference was generated by a significant fraction of SNr neurons (Figure 2A, bottom).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The difference in firing rates between Maybe-Stop-Contra and No-Stop conditions was generated by a significant fraction of SNr neurons.
source: Average firing rates were significantly higher in the Maybe-Stop-Contra condition (Figure 2A, top), and this difference was generated by a significant fraction of SNr neurons (Figure 2A, bottom).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Elevated SNr firing with action restraint was not observed in the sessions without significant behavioral evidence for proactive inhibition.
source: This elevated SNr firing with action restraint was not observed in the sessions without significant behavioral evidence for proactive inhibition (Figure 2A, right; 173 neurons, mean FR = 44 Hz).
evidence: This is a control comparison stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 173 neurons were recorded in sessions without significant behavioral evidence for proactive inhibition.
source: This elevated SNr firing with action restraint was not observed in the sessions without significant behavioral evidence for proactive inhibition (Figure 2A, right; 173 neurons, mean FR = 44 Hz).
evidence: This describes the sample size for control sessions.

claim: The mean firing rate of neurons in sessions without proactive inhibition was 44 Hz.
source: This elevated SNr firing with action restraint was not observed in the sessions without significant behavioral evidence for proactive inhibition (Figure 2A, right; 173 neurons, mean FR = 44 Hz).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the neural data.

claim: Decreases in SNr firing shortly before movement onset are thought to enable movements by disinhibiting downstream structures including the superior colliculus.
source: Decreases in firing shortly before movement onset are thought to enable movements, by disinhibiting downstream structures including the superior colliculus (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Both increase-type and decrease-type neurons contributed to elevated SNr activity with action restraint.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, both increase-type and decrease-type neurons contributed to elevated SNr activity with action restraint (Figure 2D, left).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was no relationship between the extent of elevated firing in Maybe-Stop trials and the firing rate change before movement onset.
source: There was no relationship between the extent of elevated firing in Maybe-Stop trials, and the firing rate change before movement onset (Figure 2D, right).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Neurons more active just before Ipsi compared to just before Contra movements ('Ipsi>Contra') showed elevated firing when Contra actions might need to be cancelled.
source: We found a significant relationship: neurons more active just before Ipsi compared to just before Contra movements ('Ipsi>Contra') showed elevated firing when Contra actions might need to be cancelled (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: No relationship was found between proactive inhibition and neurons with 'Contra>Ipsi' selectivity.
source: No such relationship was found for neurons with the opposite selectivity ('Contra>Ipsi'; Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Both subtypes of 'Ipsi>Contra' cells (those that preferentially increase firing with Ipsi movements and those that preferentially decrease firing with Contra movements) had elevated firing before the Go! cue on Maybe-Stop-Contra trials.
source: We found that both subtypes had elevated firing before the Go! cue on Maybe-Stop-Contra trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overall SNr population activity showed a clear shift before the Go! cue during Maybe-Stop-Contra trials.
source: When we projected Maybe-Stop-Contra data onto these axes, we found that overall SNr population activity showed a clear shift before the Go! cue (Figure 3A, middle).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The shift in SNr population activity was especially pronounced on the Selection Axis, with a highly significant bias toward Ipsi.
source: This shift was especially pronounced on the Selection Axis, with a highly significant bias toward Ipsi (Figure 3A, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant bias on the Initiation Axis toward movement.
source: There was also a significant bias on the Initiation Axis (toward movement).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ipsi>Contra cells showed a strong Selection Axis bias, without a significant Initiation Axis bias.
source: Ipsi>Contra cells showed a strong Selection Axis bias, without a significant Initiation Axis bias (Figure 3B), and the converse was seen for Contra>Ipsi cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Contra>Ipsi cells showed a significant Initiation Axis bias without a Selection Axis bias.
source: Ipsi>Contra cells showed a strong Selection Axis bias, without a significant Initiation Axis bias (Figure 3B), and the converse was seen for Contra>Ipsi cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Trajectories during wrong choice trials were biased both toward Ipsi action and toward initiation at the time of Go! cue.
source: Trajectories during wrong choice trials were biased both toward Ipsi action and toward initiation at the time of Go! cue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), consistent with our prior GPe results (Gu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Trials in which rats failed to initiate actions (limited hold violations) did not show any statistically significant bias at the Go! cue time.
source: Trials in which rats failed to initiate actions (limited hold violations) did not show any statistically significant bias at the Go! cue time, although after the Go! cue the neural trajectory showed movement in the direction away from action initiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: After the Go! cue, the neural trajectory on limited hold violation trials showed movement in the direction away from action initiation.
source: Trials in which rats failed to initiate actions (limited hold violations) did not show any statistically significant bias at the Go! cue time, although after the Go! cue the neural trajectory showed movement in the direction away from action initiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Movement slowing in PD has been associated with changes in basal ganglia firing patterns.
source: Movement slowing in PD has been associated with changes in basal ganglia firing patterns (Sharott et al., 2014; Tai, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurons recorded in sessions with significant proactive inhibition behavior showed more irregular and bursty firing compared to neurons in sessions that did not.
source: Neurons recorded in sessions with significant proactive inhibition behavior (n=446) showed more irregular and bursty firing compared to neurons (n=173) in sessions that did not (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The degree of irregularity was correlated with the mean session-wide RTs.
source: The degree of irregularity was correlated with the mean session-wide RTs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased irregularity and bursting were seen during Maybe-Stop-Contra trials compared to No-Stop trials, selectively in sessions with a significant proactive inhibition effect.
source: Increased irregularity and bursting were also seen during Maybe-Stop-Contra trials compared to No-Stop trials; this occurred selectively in those sessions with a significant proactive inhibition effect (Figure 4D, left), and not those without (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The degree of increased irregularity between conditions was correlated with the magnitude of the proactive effect on RTs on each session.
source: Moreover, the degree of increased irregularity between conditions was correlated with the magnitude of the proactive effect on RTs on each session (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Engaging proactive inhibition increases spiking variability both within- and between-sessions.
source: Together, these results show that engaging proactive inhibition increases spiking variability both within- and between-sessions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings in Figure 4.

claim: More variable SNr inter-spike intervals within-trials were associated with more variable trajectories through a more variable network state at Go! cue, and longer and more variable RTs.
source: More variable SNr inter-spike intervals within-trials were associated with more variable trajectories through a more variable network state at Go! cue, and longer and more variable RTs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the trajectory variability analysis.

claim: Decreases in spike variability have been previously linked to stimulus onset in the cortex.
source: In the cortex, decreases in spike variability have been previously linked to various processes including stimulus onset (Churchland et al., 2010), attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009), and movement preparation (Churchland et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Decreases in spike variability have been previously linked to attention in the cortex.
source: In the cortex, decreases in spike variability have been previously linked to various processes including stimulus onset (Churchland et al., 2010), attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009), and movement preparation (Churchland et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Decreases in spike variability have been previously linked to movement preparation in the cortex.
source: In the cortex, decreases in spike variability have been previously linked to various processes including stimulus onset (Churchland et al., 2010), attention (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009), and movement preparation (Churchland et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There is evidence of within-trial changes in spike variability in the striatum.
source: There is also evidence of within-trial changes in spike variability in the striatum (Berke, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There are no prior observations of specific task cues evoking increases in variability between or within trials.
source: To our knowledge, there are no prior observations of specific task cues evoking increases in variability between or within trials.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: There was a strong relationship between CV of individual neurons and their corresponding population trajectory variability.
source: As expected, there was a strong relationship between CV of individual neurons and their corresponding population trajectory variability (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Trajectory variability was significantly increased by proactive inhibition.
source: Furthermore, trajectory variability was significantly increased by proactive inhibition (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Trajectory variability increased during the hold period (examining the 0.8 s epoch just before the Go! cue, excluding trials with hold duration <0.8 s, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.003).
source: Trajectory variability increased during the hold period (examining the 0.8 s epoch just before the Go! cue, excluding trials with hold duration <0.8 s, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.003), and was also observed even beforehand (0.8 s epoch before Nose In, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from trajectory variability analysis.

claim: Trajectory variability was observed even before the hold period (0.8 s epoch before Nose In, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.003).
source: Trajectory variability increased during the hold period (examining the 0.8 s epoch just before the Go! cue, excluding trials with hold duration <0.8 s, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.003), and was also observed even beforehand (0.8 s epoch before Nose In, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from trajectory variability analysis.

claim: The increase in within-trial trajectory variability with proactive inhibition resulted in a more variable state-space position at the time of Go! cue onset, across trials.
source: This increase in within-trial trajectory variability with proactive inhibition indeed resulted in a more variable state-space position at the time of Go! cue onset, across trials (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Variability of state-space position across trials was correlated with RT.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, this variability of state-space position across trials was correlated with RT (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Regardless of previous trial-type, Maybe-Stop-Contra trials had slower RT.
source: Regardless of previous trial-type Maybe-Stop-Contra trials had slower RT (Figure 6, top row), and an Ipsi-biased SNr state-space position (Figure 6, third row).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Regardless of previous trial-type, Maybe-Stop-Contra trials had an Ipsi-biased SNr state-space position.
source: Regardless of previous trial-type Maybe-Stop-Contra trials had slower RT (Figure 6, top row), and an Ipsi-biased SNr state-space position (Figure 6, third row).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The increased CV in SNr spiking was particularly apparent following Stop-fail trials.
source: By contrast, the increased CV in SNr spiking was particularly apparent following Stop-fail trials (Figure 6, bottom).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Increased spike variability occurs when rats are especially concerned to avoid hasty responses, having just failed to sufficiently restrain behavior on the previous trial.
source: This suggests that increased spike variability occurs when rats are especially concerned to avoid hasty responses, having just failed to sufficiently restrain behavior on the previous trial.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding about CV following Stop-fail trials.

claim: CV significantly increased after premature responses (Center-out before Go! cue).
source: Consistent with the hypothesis, CV significantly increased after premature responses (Center-out before Go! cue), but not after other types of error trials (Wrong choices, and failures to respond within the RT limit).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: CV did not significantly increase after wrong choices or failures to respond within the RT limit.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis, CV significantly increased after premature responses (Center-out before Go! cue), but not after other types of error trials (Wrong choices, and failures to respond within the RT limit).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: SNr firing is modulated by internal factors such as task context.
source: Our results add to prior evidence that, beyond simple sensory or motor correlates, SNr firing is modulated by internal factors such as task context (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983a; Lintz and Felsen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Basal ganglia activity is especially affected by changes in reward expectation.
source: Basal ganglia activity is especially affected by changes in reward expectation (Lauwereyns et al., 2002) including in SNr (Sato and Hikosaka, 2002; Yasuda and Hikosaka, 2017), producing faster RTs toward more rewarding movements.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Changes in reward expectation produce faster RTs toward more rewarding movements.
source: Basal ganglia activity is especially affected by changes in reward expectation (Lauwereyns et al., 2002) including in SNr (Sato and Hikosaka, 2002; Yasuda and Hikosaka, 2017), producing faster RTs toward more rewarding movements.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the proactive task, the Maybe-Stop direction receives rewards at a lower rate due to failures-to-Stop.
source: In our proactive task the Maybe-Stop direction receives rewards at a lower rate (due to failures-to-Stop), so asymmetrical reward expectation might be at least partially responsible for the neural and choice bias toward Ipsi movements on Maybe-Stop-Contra trials.
evidence: This is an observation about the task structure.

claim: Pre-selection of movements is known to modulate SNr activity.
source: Moreover, this bias could have produced pre-selection of the Ipsi movement, a factor also known to modulate SNr activity (Basso and Wurtz, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The slower Contra RTs on Maybe-Stop-Contra trials were not accompanied by faster Ipsi RTs.
source: However, the slower Contra RTs on Maybe-Stop-Contra trials were not accompanied by faster Ipsi RTs, suggesting that slowing of Contra movements did not result simply from a greater preparation of Ipsi movements.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral data analysis.

claim: The SNr state-space bias during proactive inhibition may arise from the 'indirect pathway' projection from GPe.
source: The SNr state-space bias during proactive inhibition may arise from the 'indirect pathway' projection from GPe, which we found to have a similar neural bias toward Ipsi movements in a prior study (Gu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior findings.

claim: Proactive inhibition caused GPe population activity to shift further away from action initiation, which was not observed for SNr.
source: However, proactive inhibition also caused GPe population activity to shift further away from action initiation, which we did not observe for SNr.
evidence: This is a comparison between current and prior findings.

claim: Proactive inhibition produced no overall change in GPe firing rates.
source: Furthermore, proactive inhibition produced no overall change in GPe firing rates, and we were not able to identify a distinct subpopulation of modulated GPe neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the same authors.

claim: The authors were not able to identify a distinct subpopulation of modulated GPe neurons.
source: Furthermore, proactive inhibition produced no overall change in GPe firing rates, and we were not able to identify a distinct subpopulation of modulated GPe neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the same authors.

claim: Recent modeling has demonstrated that the influence of the GABAergic GPe inputs over SNr neurons can be far more complex than shown in classic rate models of basal ganglia function.
source: Recent modeling has demonstrated that the influence of the GABAergic GPe inputs over SNr neurons can be far more complex (Simmons et al., 2020) than shown in classic rate models of basal ganglia function, for example, switching from inhibitory to excitatory in an activity-dependent manner (Phillips et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GPe inputs to SNr can switch from inhibitory to excitatory in an activity-dependent manner.
source: Recent modeling has demonstrated that the influence of the GABAergic GPe inputs over SNr neurons can be far more complex (Simmons et al., 2020) than shown in classic rate models of basal ganglia function, for example, switching from inhibitory to excitatory in an activity-dependent manner (Phillips et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The shift in SNr Ipsi>Contra neuron firing with proactive inhibition may reflect other basal ganglia inputs, particularly the direct pathway input from striatum, or hyperdirect via the STN.
source: Alternatively, the shift in SNr Ipsi>Contra neuron firing with proactive inhibition may reflect other basal ganglia inputs, particularly the direct pathway input from striatum, or hyperdirect via the STN (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation with citation support.

claim: Increased SNr activity while waiting for a Go! cue would enhance inhibition of movements.
source: Increased SNr activity while waiting for a Go! cue would enhance inhibition of movements, and the release of this inhibition might require longer to achieve, extending RTs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on classic models.

claim: The release of enhanced SNr inhibition might require longer to achieve, extending RTs.
source: Increased SNr activity while waiting for a Go! cue would enhance inhibition of movements, and the release of this inhibition might require longer to achieve, extending RTs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Many of the Ipsi>Contra cells with elevated firing in the Maybe-Stop condition did not have movement-related pauses, but rather increases.
source: However, many of the Ipsi>Contra cells with elevated firing in the Maybe-Stop condition did not have movement-related pauses, but rather increases (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Increasing-type SNr cells have been commonly reported.
source: Such increasing-type SNr cells have been commonly reported (Bryden et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2009; Lintz and Felsen, 2016), but their functional roles remain unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The functional roles of increasing-type SNr cells remain unclear.
source: Such increasing-type SNr cells have been commonly reported (Bryden et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2009; Lintz and Felsen, 2016), but their functional roles remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Increasing-type SNr cells may help suppress competing, alternative actions.
source: They may help suppress competing, alternative actions (Gulley et al., 2002), by acting either on downstream targets or through collateral inhibition of other SNr cells (Brown et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: SNr neurons are intrinsic pacemakers that spontaneously fire regularly even if their inputs are blocked.
source: Like GPe and STN neurons, SNr neurons are intrinsic pacemakers that spontaneously fire regularly even if their inputs are blocked (Zhou and Lee, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SNr inputs alter SNr spiking by either accelerating or delaying the occurrence of the next spike.
source: These inputs – which include the aforementioned direct and indirect pathways, and also extensive local collaterals within SNr (Brown et al., 2014; Mailly et al., 2003) – thus alter SNr spiking by either accelerating or delaying the occurrence of the next spike.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pacemaker properties and cited literature.

claim: Changes in spike time variability presumably reflect either changes in local network properties or changes in the statistics of extrinsic inputs.
source: Changes in spike time variability presumably reflect either changes in local network properties, for example, due to neuromodulation (Delaville et al., 2012) or changes in the statistics of extrinsic inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation support.

claim: Neural variability might be actively elevated as part of a behavioral strategy.
source: Our finding that variability increases with proactive inhibition – in particular following Stop-fail or premature trials – suggests that variability might be actively elevated as part of a behavioral strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Neural variability can confer behavioral advantages, such as increased flexibility.
source: This would fit with proposals that neural variability can confer behavioral advantages, such as increased flexibility (Waschke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Increased neural variability with proactive inhibition may simply reflect the absence of a reduction in variability that accompanies movement preparation.
source: Alternatively, increased neural variability with proactive inhibition may simply reflect the absence of a reduction in variability that accompanies movement preparation.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation.

claim: Preparation to stop would consist, at least in part, of less preparation to go.
source: In this way, preparation to stop would consist, at least in part, of less preparation to go.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Cognitive control strategies can operate through shifts in neural variability.
source: Either way, our results demonstrate that cognitive control strategies can operate through shifts in neural variability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Parkinson's disease is characterized by both slowed movements and elevated single-neuron spike variability.
source: Connecting single-neuron measures of variability to state-space concepts of movement preparation offers an intriguing perspective on PD, which is characterized by both slowed movements (Low et al., 2002) and elevated single-neuron spike variability (Dorval et al., 2008; Lobb, 2014; Willard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A more variable state of preparation may help explain why average RTs and movement times are slowed in PD, yet the fastest movements are still preserved.
source: A more variable state of preparation may help explain why average RTs and movement times are slowed in PD, yet the fastest movements are still preserved (Mazzoni et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation support.

claim: The fastest movements are still preserved in Parkinson's disease.
source: A more variable state of preparation may help explain why average RTs and movement times are slowed in PD, yet the fastest movements are still preserved (Mazzoni et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

source: Adult male Long-Evans rats were housed on a 12 hr/12 hr reverse light-dark cycle, with training and testing performed during the dark phase.

claim: Training and testing were performed during the dark phase.
source: Adult male Long-Evans rats were housed on a 12 hr/12 hr reverse light-dark cycle, with training and testing performed during the dark phase.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Each rat was implanted with 15 or 30 tetrodes in bundles bilaterally targeting SNr.
source: Each rat was implanted with 15 or 30 tetrodes in bundles bilaterally targeting SNr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Wide-band (0.1–9000 Hz) electrophysiological data were recorded with a sampling rate of 30,000/s using an Intan RHD2000 recording system.
source: Wide-band (0.1–9000 Hz) electrophysiological data were recorded with a sampling rate of 30,000/s using an Intan RHD2000 recording system (Intan Technologies).
evidence: This describes the recording methodology.

claim: All signals were initially referenced to a skull screw (tip-flattened) on the midline 1 mm posterior to lambda.
source: All signals were initially referenced to a skull screw (tip-flattened) on the midline 1 mm posterior to lambda.
evidence: This describes the recording methodology.

claim: For spike detection, signals were re-referenced to an electrode common average, and wavelet-filtered before thresholding.
source: For spike detection we re-referenced to an electrode common average, and wavelet-filtered (Wiltschko et al., 2008) before thresholding.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology with citation.

claim: Automatic clustering of units was performed using MountainSort followed by manual curation of clusters.
source: For spike sorting we performed automatic clustering units using MountainSort Chung et al., 2017 followed by manual curation of clusters.
evidence: This describes the spike sorting methodology with citation.

claim: Approximately every two to three sessions, screws were turned to lower tetrodes by 100–160 µm.
source: Approximately every two to three sessions, screws were turned to lower tetrodes by 100–160 µm; to avoid duplicate neurons, we did not include units from the same tetrode from multiple sessions unless the tetrodes had been moved between those sessions.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Firing rates were smoothed using a Gaussian kernel (30 ms SD) and normalized (Z-scored) using each neuron's session-wide mean and SD.
source: Firing rates were smoothed using a Gaussian kernel (30 ms SD) and normalized (Z-scored) using each neuron's session-wide mean and SD.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology.

claim: Spike bursts were detected using the Poisson surprise method with a surprise threshold of 5.
source: Spike bursts were detected using the Poisson surprise method (Legéndy and Salcman, 1985) with a surprise threshold of 5, and the burst ratio was calculated as the number of spikes fired in bursts divided by the number of all spikes in each unit.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology with citation.

claim: The burst ratio was calculated as the number of spikes fired in bursts divided by the number of all spikes in each unit.
source: Spike bursts were detected using the Poisson surprise method (Legéndy and Salcman, 1985) with a surprise threshold of 5, and the burst ratio was calculated as the number of spikes fired in bursts divided by the number of all spikes in each unit.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology.

claim: The CV of inter-spike intervals and burst ratio were calculated in each trial using a 3 s time window before the Go! cue.
source: The CV of inter-spike intervals and burst ratio were calculated in each trial using a 3 s time window before the Go! cue, and averaged across all trials (for sessions with/without proactive inhibition comparison) or across each trial type (for conditional differences).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology.
